column4: The source section hears 94:4's raised remembrance as a voice reaching listeners; this ayah sets the boundary directly: believers must not raise their voices above the Prophet's voice (لَا تَرْفَعُوا أَصْوَاتَكُمْ فَوْقَ صَوْتِ النَّبِيِّ).
The next ayah gives the converse sound: voices are lowered in the Prophet's presence (وَاغْضُضْ مِنْ أَصْوَاتِكُمْ), making audible reverence the limit of the section's raised-name image.

The source section's root ذ ك ر holds both elevated renown and remembrance within oneself; this ayah explicitly joins inward remembrance (فِي نَفْسِكَ) to prayerful fear and speech below public loudness (دُونَ الْجَهْرِ).
The section turns the sound of zikr toward quiet supplication; this command says to call on one's Lord humbly and privately (تَضَرُّعًا وَخُفْيَةً), giving that inward register a direct form.
The section's remembrance includes prayer and a raised voice; here prayer is neither shouted nor wholly suppressed (وَلَا تَجْهَرْ بِصَلَاتِكَ وَلَا تُخَافِتْ بِهَا), but placed between the two.

The source section moves from animal cries to a finer camel-driver's song; this ayah names the donkey's voice as the most disagreeable sound (أَنْكَرَ الْأَصْوَاتِ لَصَوْتُ الْحَمِيرِ) and commands lowering one's voice, a specific boundary for animal sound.

The source section's root ر ف ع links elevation to voice and the honor of ذكر; this ayah says good speech rises to God (الْكَلِمُ الطَّيِّبُ يَصْعَدُ إِلَيْهِ), joining verbal sound to elevation while locating honor with God.

The section brings a listener onto the sound of a creaking back and then remembrance; here riders settle on animals' backs (ظُهُورِهِ) and remember their Lord's favor (ذَكَرْتُمْ نِعْمَةَ رَبِّكُمْ), meeting the saddle scene with spoken gratitude.

The mounted riders' utterance in 43:13 ends by saying they will return to their Lord (إِنَّا إِلَىٰ رَبِّنَا لَمُنقَلِبُونَ); that return gives a voiced form to this section's final turn of longing toward the Lord.

The section evokes a caravan's finer riding-song and a name carried far; here Abraham is told to announce the pilgrimage (وَأَذِّنْ فِي النَّاسِ بِالْحَجِّ), after which people arrive on foot and lean camels from distant passes.

The pilgrims summoned in 22:27 are to mention God's name over the livestock provided for them (وَيَذْكُرُوا اسْمَ اللَّهِ); the ayah joins the section's traveling-animal scene to voiced remembrance in its own ritual context.
The section's creaking saddle and animal sounds meet a ritual camel scene: over the camels standing in rows, people are commanded to mention God's name (فَاذْكُرُوا اسْمَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهَا صَوَافَّ).

The adjacent 22:36 names God over sacrificial camels; this ayah says their flesh and blood do not reach God, but piety does, a boundary that illuminates the section's shift from a publicly heard name to inward remembrance.

This ayah places the two dictionary branches named in the section together: houses are permitted to be raised (تُرْفَعَ) and God's name mentioned and glorified in them (وَيُذْكَرَ فِيهَا اسْمُهُ). The raising is literal here, with voiced worship inside.

The section's 94:7–8 turn from completed work toward the Lord meets people whom trade does not distract from remembrance, prayer, and almsgiving (عَن ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ وَإِقَامِ الصَّلَاةِ); 24:36 supplies the neighboring setting of raised houses and praise.

The section names eagle and chicken cries and then remembrance as prayer and praise; this ayah says birds and all in the heavens and earth know their prayer and glorification (تَسْبِيحَهُ), directly meeting animal voice with praise.
The section's animal sound meets an explicit singing-like scene: mountains and birds are told to echo with David (أَوِّبِي مَعَهُ وَالطَّيْرَ), making animal voice a form of praise.
This repeated David scene says the mountains echo praise with him at evening and sunrise (أَوِّبِي مَعَهُ); 38:19 names the assembled birds, completing the animal-voice scene in the next ayah.
The birds assembled around David, each returning in praise (وَالطَّيْرَ مَحْشُورَةً), supply the animal voices adjacent to 38:18's mountains echoing with him.
In another account of David, mountains and birds glorify with him (يُسَبِّحْنَ مَعَ دَاوُودَ); this specifically joins the section's bird sounds to its dictionary sense of remembrance as praise.

The section asks the reader to hear animal sound as part of its sound-world; this ayah says all things glorify God, though humans do not understand their glorification (لَا تَفْقَهُونَ تَسْبِيحَهُمْ), giving that sound a limit of intelligibility.

The section's final desire is directed to the Lord, and it names ذكر as spoken remembrance; this command says to remember the Lord's name and devote oneself wholly to Him (وَتَبَتَّلْ إِلَيْهِ تَبْتِيلًا).

The section joins remembrance, praise, and elevation; this command explicitly says to glorify the name of the Lord Most High (سَبِّحِ اسْمَ رَبِّكَ الْأَعْلَىٰ), a close meeting of name, praise, and height.

The source section's dictionary sense of ذكر includes prayer and praise; this ayah says the successful person remembers the Lord's name and prays (وَذَكَرَ اسْمَ رَبِّهِ فَصَلَّىٰ), joining those acts in sequence.

The section describes remembrance as prayer and as sound; here the call to Friday prayer (نُودِيَ لِلصَّلَاةِ) is followed by a command to hasten to God's remembrance (فَاسْعَوْا إِلَىٰ ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ), explicitly joining call and dhikr.

After prayer, people disperse, seek God's bounty, and remember Him much (وَاذْكُرُوا اللَّهَ كَثِيرًا); this gives a concrete parallel to the section's sequence of finishing one task and turning toward the Lord, following 62:9's call.
The section turns from a name carried aloud to inward remembrance; Zakariya's prayer is described as a hidden call (نِدَاءً خَفِيًّا), directly staging supplication in a quiet voice.

Before 7:205's inward remembrance below public loudness, this neighboring ayah commands listeners to hear the recitation and be silent (فَاسْتَمِعُوا لَهُ وَأَنصِتُوا), giving the section's ear a listening scene.
The section names the creaking of saddles and howdahs; this ayah pictures a donkey carrying books (الْحِمَارِ يَحْمِلُ أَسْفَارًا), a specific loaded-animal counterpart to that traveling gear.

The section evokes a caravan's burdened backs and saddles; this ayah says riding animals carry people's loads to distant lands (تَحْمِلُ أَثْقَالَكُمْ إِلَىٰ بَلَدٍ), closely matching the loaded journey.

The section reads ذِكر as honor carried beyond the moment; Abraham asks for a truthful tongue among later generations (لِسَانَ صِدْقٍ فِي الْآخِرِينَ), a prayer for a name that endures in people's speech.
This ayah says God gave the prophets a lofty, truthful tongue (لِسَانَ صِدْقٍ عَلِيًّا); it makes the section's raised remembrance as lasting honor concrete in the reputation granted among people.

The section's ذكر includes prayer and praise, and its focus is the Prophet's raised mention; this ayah commands believers to bless and greet the Prophet (صَلُّوا عَلَيْهِ وَسَلِّمُوا), giving that honor a communal spoken form.
The section hears a name raised through speech; this command to proclaim the Lord's favor (فَحَدِّثْ) makes speaking what was received a specific counterpart to an elevated remembrance.

The section asks the reader to hear the Prophet's name; this passage depicts people calling him from behind the chambers (يُنَادُونَكَ مِن وَرَاءِ الْحُجُرَاتِ), the same vocal setting as 49:2's rule on voices.

The callers in 49:4 are told that waiting until the Prophet comes out would be better for them; this ayah completes the boundary between clamorous calling and respectful address beside 49:2's voice instruction.

The source section makes a back-bearing burden audible and then says it is lifted; this verse depicts wrongdoers carrying their burdens on their backs (أَوْزَارَهُمْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ), a specific reverse in which the burden remains.

The source section's dictionary account of root ن ق ض names sounds of fingers and joints; this ayah singles out fingertips (بَنَانَهُ) as bodily detail God can reassemble, though it does not itself describe a sound.

Zakariya says his bones have weakened (وَهَنَ الْعَظْمُ), a bodily counterpart to the strained back and ribs in the section; beside 19:3's hidden prayer, this weakness is voiced as a petition, though no creaking is stated.
The section names supplication as one sense of ذكر; here God says He is near and answers the supplicant when called (دَعْوَةَ الدَّاعِ إِذَا دَعَانِ), giving that prayerful address its own context.
The source section's dictionary gloss says ذكر includes prayer; this command explicitly pairs establishing prayer with remembrance of God (وَأَقِمِ الصَّلَاةَ لِذِكْرِي).

The section contrasts an elevated, heard name with inward remembrance; this ayah distinguishes speech spoken aloud from the secret and what is still more hidden (السِّرَّ وَأَخْفَى), giving the sound boundary a divine listener.

The section's raised and inward registers meet this statement that God knows speech kept secret or spoken aloud (أَسِرُّوا قَوْلَكُمْ أَوِ اجْهَرُوا بِهِ), while the ayah locates that speech's knowledge in hearts.

The section asks a reader to hear the raised remembrance; this ayah calls the reminder useful to one who has a heart or lends an ear (وَأَلْقَى السَّمْعَ وَهُوَ شَهِيدٌ), specifying receptive listening.

The section's name and remembrance are sounds that reach a hearer; here hearts tremble when God is mentioned and faith increases when verses are recited (وَجِلَتْ قُلُوبُهُمْ), a specific bodily response to remembrance.

The section links sound with bodily sensation; this ayah describes the revealed discourse making the skins of those who fear God shiver and then their skins and hearts soften at His remembrance (تَقْشَعِرُّ ... جُلُودُهُمْ), a concrete bodily response to recitation.

The section ends with desire turning toward the Lord and inward remembrance; this ayah says hearts find rest in God's remembrance (بِذِكْرِ اللَّهِ تَطْمَئِنُّ الْقُلُوبُ), specifying the inward effect.

The source section reads ذكر as honor and a name carried among people; this ayah calls the revealed Book a mention for its audience (فِيهِ ذِكْرُكُمْ), a distinct scriptural use that makes the honor/reminder sense explicit.

The source section's root ذ ك ر spans remembrance and honor; this ayah calls the revealed message a reminder for the Prophet and his people (لَذِكْرٌ لَّكَ وَلِقَوْمِكَ), then says they will be questioned about it.

The source section uses ذكر for voiced honor and prayer; this ayah calls the revelation a reminder (تَذْكِرَةٌ), the written/revealed sense of the same source root, distinct from the section's audible reputation.

The reminder named in 80:11 is described here as elevated and purified (مَرْفُوعَةٍ مُّطَهَّرَةٍ); neighboring 80:13 identifies the honored sheets, giving a physical counterpart to the section's raised ذكر rather than the same vocal scene.
This ayah says Noah was left among later generations (وَتَرَكْنَا عَلَيْهِ فِي الْآخِرِينَ); that enduring remembrance is a concrete parallel to the section's honor carried beyond the moment.
This repeated legacy formula says Abraham was left among later generations (وَتَرَكْنَا عَلَيْهِ فِي الْآخِرِينَ), a specific instance of a name enduring in later people's memory.
This repeated legacy formula says Moses and Aaron were left among later generations (وَتَرَكْنَا عَلَيْهِمَا فِي الْآخِرِينَ), making the section's lasting honor recur for another pair of prophets.
This repeated legacy formula says Elijah was left among later generations (وَتَرَكْنَا عَلَيْهِ فِي الْآخِرِينَ), another concrete instance of remembrance outlasting the one remembered.

This ayah places the revelation in honored sheets (فِي صُحُفٍ مُّكَرَّمَةٍ); neighboring 80:14 says they are raised and purified, giving the section's raised remembrance a material written counterpart.

The section names a fine caravan song and separately says ذكر can mean prayer and praise; this ayah sharply contrasts worship with whistling and handclapping (إِلَّا مُكَاءً وَتَصْدِيَةً), marking vocal noise as an empty substitute for prayer.
The section's sound carries a name to listeners; here opponents tell one another not to listen to the Quran and to make noise over it (وَالْغَوْا فِيهِ), a deliberate attempt to block hearing.

The source section says its song sense resembles the camel-driver's chant; uncertainly, this ayah's image of someone calling to animals that hear only a call and shout (دُعَاءً وَنِدَاءً) marks what such a riding-call can sound like to its animal audience.

The source section's root ذ ك ر moves between public honor and inward remembrance; this ayah gives remembrance a reciprocal form, commanding people to remember God with the promise that He will remember them.

The section ends with desire turned toward the Lord and remembrance held inwardly; this ayah describes people calling their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face (يَدْعُونَ رَبَّهُم بِالْغَدَاةِ وَالْعَشِيِّ يُرِيدُونَ وَجْهَهُ), a specific form of that orientation.

This repeated caller scene says people call their Lord morning and evening desiring His face; it contrasts them with someone whose heart is heedless of God's remembrance and follows desire, sharpening the section's turn from public renown to inward longing.

This ayah names horses, mules, and donkeys made for riding and adornment; neighboring 16:7 describes animals carrying loads to distant lands, giving the section's saddle and caravan song a specific riding scene.

The section names bird and poultry cries as an animal branch of its sound image; Solomon says he was taught the speech of birds (مَنطِقَ الطَّيْرِ), a specific case where an animal voice carries intelligible speech.

An ant speaks and warns its community (قَالَتْ نَمْلَةٌ), and Solomon hears and smiles at her words; this gives the section's animal-sound detail a precise scene of a small creature's voice reaching a listener.

After hearing the ant in 27:18, Solomon turns to prayer, asking his Lord to enable gratitude (رَبِّ أَوْزِعْنِي أَنْ أَشْكُرَ); this joins the section's animal voice to its movement toward remembrance and praise.

The section hears words as sound and tracks what a listening ear receives; this ayah depicts people falling in prostration when the revealed verses are recited to them, a specific bodily response to voiced revelation.
Those listeners answer the recitation in 17:107 by glorifying their Lord (سُبْحَانَ رَبِّنَا); this is a spoken praise following heard revelation, matching the section's sense of ذكر as praise.
The listeners in 17:107 fall on their faces weeping and grow in humility; this ayah supplies the bodily response that completes the recitation scene, alongside the section's body-and-sound image.

The section's raised remembrance is meant to reach an ear; this ayah describes a covering over hearts and deafness in ears, then says that when the Lord alone is mentioned in the Quran, some turn away, a direct reversal of hearing.

The section ends with desire directed to the Lord; this ayah pictures people rising from their beds to call their Lord in fear and hope (يَدْعُونَ رَبَّهُمْ خَوْفًا وَطَمَعًا), giving that inward orientation a bodily and vocal setting.

The section compares a fine riding song with remembrance and prayer; this command to recite the Quran in measured recitation (وَرَتِّلِ الْقُرْآنَ تَرْتِيلًا) gives a specific, deliberate mode of voiced sacred words.
